main.text: [III, 211] CHAPTER XIII. [col. 421]
It is proved that שרף saraph is the hydrus and chersydrus; those bitten by which, the Israelites, were healed by the sight of the bronze serpent.

The שרף saraph also deserves our discussion, since it was a type of Christ, Num 21:9. John 3:14, and since it shares its name with the noblest of the angels, Isa 6:2. Moreover, it alone among serpents is said to fly, Isa 14:29 (var. XV, 2.) and XXX, 6. There מעופף refers to true flight, not to leaping, as the Hebrews wrongly write. The Sacred Writers mention two places in which it chiefly breeds, namely Arabia Deserta, Deut 8:15, and Egypt, Isa 30:6. The name is derived from burning: either because of its fiery colour, which the bronze serpent would have reproduced (so Vatablus), or because it burns with its breath and bite. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], on Numbers XXI: את הנחשים השרפים ששורפים את האדם בארס שיניהם, The serpents were called seraphim because they burned a man with the poison of their teeth. And on Es. XXX, of the serpent saraph: וזרק להב מפיו, It scatters flame from its mouth. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon: נקראים כן לפי שהם שורפים בהבל פיהם, They are so called because they burn with the breath of their mouth. For a not dissimilar reason those angels were called שרפים seraphim (that is, as Dionysius ^{a)} and Cyril ^{b)} interpret it, ἐμπρησταὶ, ἤτοι θερμαίνοντες [emprēstai, ētoi thermainontes]), one of whom cleansed the lips of the prophet Isaiah with a coal taken from the altar. The Greeks, too, name certain serpents πρηστῆρας [prēstēras] and καύσωνας [kausōnas], likewise from burning. This was the reason why certain recent interpreters [col. 422] rendered the Hebrew שרף saraph as prester and causon, words which correspond exactly to the Hebrew if one considers their origin. For anyone who compares the versions of the Greeks with the source will at once notice that the verb שרף is the same as ἐμπρῆσαι [emprēsai] or κατακαῦσαι [katakausai]. But one must not cling so stubbornly to etymologies [III, 212] that the thing itself is meanwhile neglected. Since it is common to very different serpents that they burn with breath or bite, why could a name taken from this not apply to various species of serpents? What of the fact that the Greeks themselves do not know what kind of serpent the prester is? For some confuse the prester with the dipsas, as Dioscorides and Aegineta do; others make it distinct, as Lucan and Solinus do. And what Aelian thought here nobody could easily say, since in one place he seems to side with Dioscorides, in another with Lucan. Therefore those who interpret שרף saraph by so doubtful and ambiguous a word rather obscure the matter than explain it.

To me, weighing everything, it seems most probable that שרף saraph is the hydrus or chersydrus. These two differ little from each other. For what had been a hydrus in winter, while there was water in the pools, is forced to live on dry land after the water has failed in the heat, and so becomes a chersydrus, that is, a hydrus living ἐν χέρσῳ [en chersō], on dry land. Then indeed, tormented by thirst in hot regions, it has a far sharper and more harmful poison. Hence the Poet ^{c)}:
After the marsh is drained and the earth gapes with heat, it leaps out onto the dry ground and, rolling its flaming eyes, rages in the fields, fierce with thirst and maddened by the heat.

Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 35: The chersydrus, living on land, becomes fiercer than itself. In moist places, sated with moist food, it does not have pure poison; but when it is terrestrial, it acquires it in its most undiluted and more harmful form. Therefore it then burns up with its bite whatever it touches. Nicander on those bitten by the chersydrus, Theriaca, line 363:
— — — τὰ δ' ἄλγεα φωτὰ δαμάζει Μυρία πυρπολέοντα· θοῶς δ' ἐπὶ γυῖα χέονται Πρηδόνες. — — — — — [ta d' algea phōta damazei / Myria pyrpoleonta; thoōs d' epi guia cheontai / Prēdones.]

Countless pains overpower the men, ravaging them as with fires; and at once burning pustules spread over the limbs. For that is properly πρηδόνες [prēdones]. Aëtius: In those bitten there occurs swelling, continuous burning pain, etc. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] ^{d)}: تاخذ اللسعة بوجع شديد وتلتهب [taʾkhudh al-lasʿa bi-wajaʿ shadīd wa-taltahib] The bite begins with violent pain, and becomes inflamed. Others in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] report that on a rod brought to its mouth blisters are raised, or pustules of the colour of bile; and that a sword, from the point to the hilt, is stained a foul blue colour, as if seized by a violent flame; likewise that this poison has a fiery force, and therefore always seeks the upper parts. The poets imagine that Hercules was consumed by this fire when he had put on a garment dipped in the poison of the Lernaean Hydra. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 9, Fable 3: [III, 213] The very blood hisses, as a glowing plate once dipped in a cold pool, and boils with the burning poison. There is no limit: the greedy flames suck up his vitals, dark-blue sweat flows from his whole body, his scorched sinews crackle, the devouring fire roams in the depths of his lungs and feeds through all his limbs.
And Hercules himself in Seneca, Hercules Oetaeus, line 1216.
Alas! What scorpion within, what crab, turned back and fixed in me with burning wound, scorches my marrow? — — —
See the rest there, and more on the same theme in Sophocles, in the Trachiniae, where even the fleece dyed with this poison is eaten away and consumed as if by a hidden fire ^{e)}:
Τοῦτ' ἠφάνισαι διάβορον πρὸς οὐδενὸς Τῶν ἔνδων, ἀλλ' ἐδεστὸν ἐξ αὐτοῦ φθίνει. [Tout' ēphanisai diaboron pros oudenos Tōn endōn, all' edeston ex autou phthinei.] [col. 423]
Although these things are exaggerated, as is the custom of poets, they nevertheless show abundantly that the name שרף saraph, that is, ἐμπρηστοῦ [emprēstou], suits this evil most of all.

But what moves me above all to believe that שרף saraph is the hydrus is that I see Egypt called in Isa 30:6 the land from which comes the viper, ושרף מעופף, and the flying Saraph: namely the winged serpents which, as Cicero ^{f)} and Josephus ^{g)} write, fly into Egypt from Libya; as Herodotus ^{h)}, Mela ^{i)}, Lucan ^{k)}, Solinus ^{l)}, Ammianus ^{m)} write, from Arabia; and as Aelian writes, from both regions ^{n)}. These had the appearance of hydri ^{R1}. The matter is stated explicitly in Herodotus ^{o)}: Τοῦ δ' ὄφιος ἡ μορφὴ, οἵηπερ τῶν ὕδρων [Tou d' opheos hē morphē, hoiēper tōn hydrōn]; The form of the serpent is like that of the hydri. To this belongs the fact that Cicero calls them angues [snakes], that is, water serpents. And Lucilius, book 23,

— — portents, and winged snakes. [III, 214] So also Solinus and Ammianus, who likewise, following Mela, report that they emerge from marshes. So it is now plain to everyone that the kind of winged serpents belongs to the species of the hydri. You will ask where Isidore gets the statement that they are called Sirens. In Arabia, he says, there are serpents with wings, which are called Sirens, which not only run faster than horses but are even said to fly. Someone might think this an Arabic word. But in the writings of the Arabs I have found only two names for winged serpents, very far removed from this one: namely سف [sf] and اعرجات [aʿrajāt]. And what this is will be told in the chapter On the Dragon.
If there should be anyone who, with the Hebrews, thinks that the flying saraph in Isaiah is the acontias, and that by flight nothing but a leap is meant, in the sense in which Lucan said,
— — — and the flying javelin-snakes,

as though what we read in the ancients about winged snakes were fables, let him know that the fact is confirmed by many in our age: and that in France itself, among the Bigerrones by the Pyrenees, there is a kind of snake from whose sides cartilages spread out in the manner and appearance of wings. So Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] against Cardano, Exercitation 183. And Brodaeus, Miscellanea, book 3, chapter 1, records one in the territory of the Santones struck down by a peasant's hoe as it flew at him, and presented to King Francis. Cardano too, De Varietate rerum, book 7, chapter 29, writes that he saw in Paris five two-footed serpents with tiny wings, but brought from India; in which country Megasthenes had long ago described winged snakes, in Aelian, book 16, chapter 41. And Odoardo Barbosa, treating of the mountain that divides Malabar and Narsinga: Vi si trouano serpe con ali, molto velenose, che volano: delli quali è fama, che col fiato è la guardatura ammazano, quei che vi, si pongono troppo appresso. That is, There winged and flying serpents are found, very poisonous, which are reported to kill with their breath and gaze those who come too near. Scaliger copied this almost word for word against Cardano, Exercitation 183, chapter 5. And Vincent le Blanc, Part 1 of the Travels, chapter 25: East of Lake Chiamay there are great forests and vast marshes, to which the journey is dangerous, because very large serpents live there which, lifted from the ground as if by bats' wings and supported on the tip of their tail, are carried along very swiftly. They say these once existed in such numbers around these places that they almost depopulated the neighbouring province. And below: I saw some of them of immense bulk, which, when hungry, attack sheep and other cattle ^{R2}.

[III, 215] I cannot help adding that the flying saraph is placed by the Hebrews among those animals whose odour is noxious. Porta Coeli fol. 24a b.: ויש מקצת בעלי חיים שיצא ארס גדול וריח רע וחזק מפיהם כמין זאב ומין שרף מעופף, And there are certain animals from whose mouth comes much poison and a bad and heavy odour, such as the wolf and the flying saraph. And again: ושרף מעופף שורף האויר המעפש ההוא כל קרוב אליו, And the flying saraph, scorching the air, infects everything that is near it. [col. 424] From this a new argument arises to prove that the saraph belongs to the kind of the hydri. For of them the greatest Poet says,
— — — with foul-breathing hydri.

And Aelian, History, book 8, chapter 13: Περὶ Κόρκυραν δὲ γίνονται καλέμεναι ὕδραι· αἵπερουν τοὺς διώκοντας (read πρὸς τοὺς διώκοντας) ἐπιστραφεῖσαι, καὶ φυσήσασαι πνεῦμα ἄτομον, εἶτα ἀναστέλλουσι τῆς ὁρμῆς, καὶ ἀποστρέφουσι [Peri Korkyran de ginontai kalemenai hydrai· haiperoun tous diōkontas (pros tous diōkontas) epistrapheisai, kai physēsasai pneuma atomon, eita anastellousi tēs hormēs, kai apostrephousi]. But in Corcyra hydrae are bred which, turning upon their pursuers and breathing out a heavy breath, check their onset and drive them away.

I see one possible objection: that hydri are born and reared in watery places, and it is reasonable to suppose that the desert of the Israelites lacked such places, above all in the part where they were bitten by the serpents, since these serpents were sent against them for the very reason that they had murmured against God and Moses for lack of water, Num 21:5–6. But this objection can be met in several ways. 1. Even if the Israelites, faint with thirst, lacked drinkable water, it does not at once follow that there were no marshy and muddy waters in the desert in which hydri might lurk. Nicander at any rate states that hydri mostly live ἐπὶ βροχθώδει λίμνῃ [epi brochthōdei limnē], that [III, 216] is, ἀνύδρῳ, ἢ ξηρᾷ, ἢ ὀλίγον ὕδωρ ἐχούσῃ [anydrō, ē xēra, ē oligon hydōr echousē], in a waterless lake, or a dry one, or one having little water, as the Scholiast interprets it. 2. Moreover it is known (and we have already proved it above ^{p)}) that hydri, when water fails, do not at once die but become chersydri, and by this very fact truly seraphim, that is, burning and scorching. It is probable that the same happened here, and that those serpents' bite was then more dangerous, because the heat had consumed the water even from the marshes. That this conjecture is not idle is shown by the season. For Nicander adds that hydri become chersydri and beset the roads around the Dog Days:
— — — — ὅταν ὕδωρ Σείριος ἀζήνῃσι, τρύγη δ' ἐνὶ πυθμένι λίμνης· [— — — — hotan hydōr Seirios azēnēsi, trygē d' eni pythmeni limnēs·]

When the Dog Star has dried up the water, and there is dryness at the bottom of the lake. Now see and weigh, reader, at what season of the year this calamity fell upon the Israelites. Aaron died on Mount Hor on the first day of the fifth month, Num 33:38, that is, the month Ab or Abba (so read in Josephus instead of Σαββὰ [Sabba], Antiquities, book 4, chapter 4). The date corresponds to the nineteenth of July. The Israelites mourned him for thirty days, Num 20:29. Immediately there was a battle against the king of Arad. Then came the murmuring of the people and the sending of the serpents, Num. XXI. So this must have happened around the end of August, as the sun was leaving the Dog Star. 3. Finally, even granting that that part of the desert lacked water at every season of the year, watery places were nevertheless not far off. For on the first march, Num 21:10, the people came to a place called Oboth (that is, wineskins), probably because there they not only drank but also refilled the skins long empty. The second march was to Ije-abarim, that is, heaps of the fords, or, as the Chaldees explain it, the ford of those crossing. The third to the brook Zered. The fourth to the river Arnon. The fifth to Beer, that is, the well, celebrated in Scripture in splendid words, Num 21:17–18. Hence we read in Deut 10:7 that the Israelites, shortly after the death of Aaron, came into a land watered by rivers of water. So let no one imagine that this desert was everywhere dry and waterless. Hydri born in these or similar places, whether creeping or even flying, could therefore be sent by God against the Israelites. This seems to be inferable from the words of Moses, The Lord sent among the people Seraphim serpents. By these words, I say, the divine writer clearly hints that these serpents were not born there, but were summoned from elsewhere by a certain force θεηλάτῳ [theēlatō], to punish the stubborn people. Just as in Egypt the frogs, leaving their natural place, that is, the rivers, streams and marshes, covered the whole land like a cloud, so that they even climbed the upper [III, 217] storeys of the houses. Accordingly it is said of the serpents sent by God, [col. 425] Wis 16:5 Ἐπῆλθε θηρίων θυμός [Epēlthe thēriōn thymos]· The poison of serpents came upon them (as if unexpectedly).

I shall add, as a corollary, the causes that the Hebrews devise for this plague, inflicted by God on the murmuring people. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] observes that in Eccl 10:11. בעל לשון, that is, the slanderer or blasphemer, is compared by Solomon with a serpent that bites when it is not charmed. From this he infers that the biting of an insolent tongue among the Israelite people was justly punished by the bite of serpents. And perhaps this is not beside the point. For in Ps 140:4 too, slanderers are said to sharpen their tongue like serpents, and to have the poison of asps under their lips. But the Jerusalem translator, largely following Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan], seems to offer mere trifles in his paraphrase of Num 21:6 A daughter of the voice (he says, that is, an oracle) went forth from the midst of the earth, and a voice was heard on high: namely, See, all you sons of men, and listen; and hear, all you sons of flesh. I cursed the serpent from the foundation of the world, and said to it, „Dust shall be your food“. Yet it did not murmur on account of its food. But my people (the Israelites) I led out free from Egypt, and sent down to them Manna from heaven, and brought quails over from the sea, and raised up for them a well from the abyss. Yet again they murmur against me on account of the Manna, saying that their soul is distressed because of the bread, whose eating is light. Therefore the serpent shall come, which did not murmur on account of its food; and I will make it bite the people of those who murmured on account of their food. And the word of the Lord stirred up against the people burning serpents, etc. As if it were to be counted to the serpent's praise that it does not murmur against God, whom it does not know.

Our own interpreters also look for allegories here: by the bites of the burning serpents they understand the fiery darts of Satan of Ephes. VI, 16., that is, the wicked suggestions by which he kindles the heat of lust, inflicts various wounds on us, and spreads his poison through all parts of the soul. Further, just as serpents are sent against the Israelites for their contempt of the manna and their murmuring against God and Moses, Num 21:5–6., so those are deservedly handed over to Satan who neglect the word of God, signified by the manna, or who blaspheme God himself, like Hymenaeus and Alexander 1 Tim. I, 20. But just as those Israelites for whom, unconcerned about a remedy, the serpents' bites were deadly are a figure of the impenitent, who, spurning the grace of God, die in their sins, so those who flee to Moses, confessing their sins and imploring the grace of God, Num. XXI, 7., plainly signify those whom the sense of their sins and the fear of divine judgment move to sounder counsels: such as those who, pricked in their heart, say to Peter and the rest of the Apostles, What shall we do, men and brethren? Acts 2:37, and the jailer of Philippi, [III, 218] who, falling trembling at the feet of Paul and Silas, says, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? Actor. XVI, 29. 30. For their sake God commanded Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole, and promised that all who had been bitten by serpents would be healed at the sight of it. The outcome confirmed this. Nor is there any doubt that that serpent foreshadowed Christ. For so Christ himself asserts, John 3:14: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up. Many people give many reasons for the type. For instance, first, that the serpent had the form of the serpents that burned with their bite, yet not their poison, just as Christ was in the likeness of sinful flesh, Roman. VIII, 3., though free from sin. Second, that the serpent was of bronze, not gold, and cast from a baser metal, so as to show us Christ, in whom there was no form, nor comeliness, nor any beauty, that we should desire him, Isa 53:2. Third, that the divine strength of Christ is signified by the firmness and durability of bronze. Hence Iob. VI, 12.: Is my strength the strength of stones? Is my flesh of bronze? And the Poet:
I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze. [col. 426]
Fourth, of all metals bronze is the most resonant. Hence Paul, 1 Cor. XIII, 1.: γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν [gegona chalkos ēchōn]. And Claudian:
No Corybant of Cybele purified you at your birth with sounding bronze. — — —

Therefore by bronze is rightly signified Christ crucified, and the preaching of the cross, whose sound went out into all the earth, Rom 10:18. But two things above all are to be observed here. Namely, 1. that Christ was raised up onto the cross, just as the serpent was onto the pole. Hence Christ himself says, John 3:14. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up. And John 12:32. If I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all men unto me. Lifted up, that is, crucified, according to the usage of the Syriac language, in which the verb ܙܩܦ [זקף] zekaph properly means to raise up. Thus 2 Tim. IV, 15. ܛܒ ܓܝܪ ܙܩܦ ܢܦܫܗ ܠܘܩܒܠ ܡܠܝܢ [טב גיר זקף נפשה לוקבל מלין] For he greatly lifted himself up against our words. Yet it frequently occurs in the sense of crucifying: as Matth. XX, 19. ܘܢܙܩܦܘܢܝܗܝ [ונזקפוניהי], And they shall raise him up, that is, they shall crucify him: in Greek σταυρῶσαι [staurōsai]. And XXIII, 34. ܘܙܩܦܝܢ ܐܢܬܘܢ [וזקפין אנתון], And you raise up, that is, you crucify: in Greek, καὶ σταυρώσετε [kai staurōsete]. And XXVI, 2. The Son of man is betrayed ܕܢܙܕܩܦ [דנזדקף], to be raised up, that is, to be crucified: in Greek, εἰς τὸ σταυρωθῆναι [eis to staurōthēnai]. And XXVII, 22. ܢܙܕܩܦ [נזדקף], let him be raised up: in Greek, σταυρωθήτω [staurōthētō], let him be crucified. The same κατάχρησις [katachrēsis] is also familiar to the Chaldeans. [III, 219] Thus Esther. VII, 10. in the second Targum, וזקיפו ית המן על קיסא, And they raised Haman upon the wood, that is, ויתלו, and they hanged him. For so it reads in the Hebrew. And in the first Targum Esther IX, 13. the ten sons of Haman יזקפון על צליבא, let them raise up upon the gibbet, in Hebrew יתלו על העץ, let them hang upon the wood. This expression seems to have arisen from the edict of King Darius, Esd. VI, 11. Whoever shall alter this, let timber be taken from his house, וזקיף יתמחא עלוהי, and, being lifted up, let him be destroyed on it: lifted up, that is, hanged. Moreover the burnt offerings too, which in Hebrew were called עולות, that is, ὑψώσεις [hypsōseis], because they were raised upward, signified that Christ, offering himself for sins, would be exalted on the cross. This too is to be observed here: that by the mere sight of the bronze serpent, raised on the pole, the Israelites were healed of the wounds the serpents had inflicted. Namely, the wounds inflicted by the demon are perfectly healed by the sight alone of Christ lifted up on the cross. The sight, that is, of faith, which is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, and through which Moses saw him who is invisible, Heb 11:1 27. And indeed that by the sight of the serpent faith in Christ is meant is taught expressly by these words of Christ, Ioh. III, 14. 15. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. Namely, as the sight of the serpent delivered the Israelites from death, so faith in Christ delivers us, faith by which we look upon him. If any in Israel, therefore, were blind, or willingly turned their eyes away, for them there was no hope of salvation: as neither today for the unbelieving, and for those that rebel against the light, Job 24:13 and for those whose minds the god of this age has blinded, lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ should shine on them, 2 Cor 4:4. Nor were the Jews healed by another's sight, but by their own: as we live by our own faith, not by another's, Hab. II, 4. and Rom. I, 17. Yet, as even weak sight could bring salvation, so faith, though still feeble, rescues us from death, provided it is true and sincere. And as one who had once been bitten and healed by seeing the serpent, if he was bitten again, fled to the same remedy: so, if after restoration we fall into sins anew, the same faith comes to our aid as before. And a just man falls seven times, and rises up seven times, Prov 24:16. Accordingly, as the Jews, relying on so ready a help, had little fear of the bite and sting of snakes: so the believer who leans on Christ, making nothing of the assaults of demons, cries out with confidence: O death, where is thy victory? O grave, where is thy sting? 1 Cor 15:55. Yet no one [col. 427] would say that the Jews were so secure in their confidence in this medicine that they deliberately provoked the serpents to bite: so we must take care that, relying on the grace and help of Christ, we do not fall into temptations of our own accord. Rather, the devil must be resisted, so that he may flee from us, Jas 4:7.

[III, 220] From these things it is clear that the sign expressed the thing signified exceedingly well; yet the reality rises many degrees above the figure. For the bronze serpent, although a symbol of God's grace, could of itself do nothing. For he who turned to it was healed not by the thing that he saw, but by you, the Saviour of all, as the author of the book of Wisdom XVI, 7 truly says. But Christ has life hidden in himself, Coloss. III, 3, and gives life to whomever he wills, John 5:21. The sight of the serpent brought healing to the Israelites alone; faith in Christ brings it to all, for in him there is neither Jew nor Greek, but you are all one in Christ Jesus, Gal. III, 28. The bronze serpent rescued those who looked at it from the death of the body in such a way that they still remained subject to death; through Christ we are freed for ever from the death of the soul as well as of the body, as he himself teaches, John 11:26. Whoever lives and believes in me shall never die. The power of the bronze serpent lasted for a day or two; but Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and for ever, Heb 13:8. Therefore it was impious to worship the bronze serpent, and Hezekiah rightly broke in pieces so outstanding a monument of divine power when he noticed that the Israelites were burning incense to it, 2 Regum XVIII, 4. But all honour the Son, just as they honour the Father, John 5:23. And all the angels worship him, Heb 1:6. And God has highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, Phil. II, 9. 10. Accordingly, whereas the bronze serpent which the Israelites worshipped was broken in pieces, on the contrary those will be broken in pieces who refuse to Christ the worship due to him. Ps 2:9. You shall break them with a rod of iron, and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel. And Dan. II, 44, of the kingdom of Christ: It shall crush and consume all those kingdoms, but it shall itself stand for ever. And in the parable, Luc. XIX, 27: Those enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slay them before me.

Moses does not say in exactly what place the bronze serpent was set up; but he relates that the Israelites, setting out from there, encamped in Oboth, Num 21:10. From this it follows that the place was פינון Phinon, or פונון Phunon, of which see Gen 36:41. Num 38:42–43. and 1 Chr 1:52. For setting out from Phunon they encamped in Oboth, Num 33:43. This, moreover, was a place in Idumaea very famous for its copper mines, as is clear from the Fathers, who write Phaeno, Phennen, Fenon and Metallo-fenon; and hence Phaenesia or Phennesia metalla [the Phaenesian or Phennesian mines]. Thus in Eusebius, book 8 of the History, ch. 13, Sylvanus, bishop of the churches around Gaza, and thirty-nine others were beheaded κατὰ τὰ ἐν Φαινοῖ χαλκοῦ μέταλλα [kata ta en Phainoi chalkou metalla], at the copper mines which are in Phaeno. And in Athanasius' Letter To the Solitaries it is related that Eutychius εἰς μέταλλον ἀποσταλῆναι, καὶ μέταλλον οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὸ τῆς [eis metallon apostalēnai, kai metallon ouch haplōs, all᾽ eis to tēs] [III, 221] was sent to the mine, and not merely to a mine, but to the mine of Phaeno. And in Epiphanius, on the Meletians: Meletius and many others were driven into exile, ὑπερορισθέντες ἐν τοῖς Φαινήσιος μετάλλοις [hyperoristhentes en tois Phainēsios metallois], banished to the Phaenesian mines. Theodoret, History book 4, ch. 19: Τοῖς Φεννεσίοις καὶ Προκοννησίοις παρεδίδοντο μετάλλοις [Tois Phennesiois kai Prokonnēsiois paredidonto metallois]. They were condemned to the Phennesian and Proconnesian mines. And not much later, of a certain deacon of Damasus: Τοῖς κατὰ Φέννης παρεδόθη μετάλλοις· ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα τοῦ χαλκοῦ· [Tois kata Phennēs paredothē metallois; esti de tauta tou chalkou;] He was condemned to the mines at Phennes, which are copper mines. So also Nicephorus Callistus, book 11, 28. But most explicitly Jerome in the Places: FENON, a camp of the children of Israel in the desert. It was once a city of the Princes of Edom, now a small village in the desert, where copper is dug out of the mines by condemned convicts as their punishment, between the city of Pe- [col. 428] tra and Zoara. Likewise: DEDAN is at the fourth milestone from Metallo-fenon towards the north. To the same I refer these words of Aristeas in the History of the Seventy Translators: Ἐλέγετο δὲ καὶ ἐκ τῶν παρακειμένων ὀρέων τῆς Ἀραβίας μέταλλα χαλκᾶ καὶ σιδηρᾶ συνίστασθαι πρότερον· ἐκλέλειπται δὲ ταῦτα, καθ᾽ ὃν ἐπεκράτησαν χρόνον Πέρσαι [Elegeto de kai ek tōn parakeimenōn oreōn tēs Arabias metalla chalka kai sidēra synistasthai proteron; ekleleiptai de tauta, kath᾽ hon epekratēsan chronon Persai]. It was also said that formerly copper and iron ores were dug from the mountains of Arabia neighbouring (Judaea), but that these had failed (that is, had been neglected, as is clear from what follows) at the time when the Persians held power. From these mines, it seems, was taken the bronze from which the bronze serpent was cast. And perhaps this was not without a mystery. For in this way it could be signified that the body which Christ assumed was not brought from elsewhere, but was born and formed in the very place where he was manifested in the flesh.

notes.text: Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] writes that in Egypt he saw the whole preserved bodies of certain winged serpents which have feet and are said to fly from Arabia into Egypt, Observations book 2, ch. 70, p. 133 (in the Sylloge Itinerarior. edited by Paulus, vol. 1, p. 238). But one should read what a certain learned man has remarked on that passage of Belon in the Notarum Mantissa appended to the second part of the said Sylloge, p. 264. Compare also our note 2 below.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde], Vermischte Sammlungen fasc. 6, ch. 7, p. 71 ff., has collected the reports of others on winged serpents. He rightly points out, however, that the serpents flying with membranous wings of which ancient and more recent writers speak are flying lizards, [III, 215] which Linnaeus (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 3, p. 1056, 13th ed.) calls dracones [dragons], and who in the Amoenitt. Academm. fasc. 1, p. 126, also described the Lacerta cauda tereti, pedibus pentadactylis, alis femore connexis, crista gulae triplici [lizard with a rounded tail, five-toed feet, wings joined to the thigh, and a threefold crest on the throat]. — Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. 6, p. 2353, sees here too his cerastes or regulus, interpreting the name שרף as noble or prince, comparing the Arabic شرف [sharufa], he was noble. He thinks the name prince was given to the cerastes from the horns or feelers that distinguish this kind of serpent, which seemed to present the appearance of a crown. So in Michaelis' opinion the cerastes bore three names among the Hebrews: 1. צפע, 2. שפיפון, 3. שרף. But he confuses the coronella with the cerastes; see our note 1 above on the preceding Chapter. We, however, have seen that only שפיפון is the cerastes cornutus, and צפע the coronella petola; while that שרף is to be referred to the dracones or flying lizards is suggested by the passages Isa 14:29. XXX, 6., where the שרף is expressly called flying or winged, מעופף. As for Michaelis' referring our שרף to the Arabic شرف [sharufa], he was noble, he seems not to have observed the usage of the verb שרף among the Hebrews, which always occurs solely in the sense of burning.
